Revenge Porn

By: Jo Munnik | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Before you take that nude selfie to send to your partner or film yourself having sex.. think very carefully .. Your most private moment could end being used as revenge porn and posted online.

Summary:
The internet defies the law that what goes up must come down.. And many women are learning (the very hard way) that once explicit media of your most private moments goes up, it may never come down.

Revenge porn is the unauthorized sharing of sexualized images, this happens most commonly across digital platforms. It is also largely categorized as digital sexual assault. It has become one of the most popular ways that disgruntled exes are taking out their anger on their former partners - by leaking their most private photos or videos online - naming and shaming the victims and sometimes even tagging the name of the company they work for and to their profiles on Facebook and Linked In etc.
95% of the victims are women. As with offline violence against women, the bulk of the abuse is at the hands not of strangers, but of people known to the women targeted. In the case of both of our case studies, their offenders were their former partners.

There are 2000 sites dedicated to revenge porn. From myex.com (where men can post pics of their exes) to shesahomewrecker.com (where women name and shame their partners mistresses and it's run by a woman).

The online world is being used as a weapon and the victims incur huge social, financial, psychological, emotional and professional costs. There are incidents of victims losing their jobs, receiving rape threats, having to move and even having to change their name.

Revenge porn cases happen all around the world, to people across all ages and the topic has started to make international mainstream news and every day conversations. Putting pressure on judiciaries and social network platforms to change laws and regulations.


Further information:
We have 3 case studies to include in the story:

LOCALLY: "SAM". (Identity must be hidden to protect her. Her ex is very dangerous).
Alice was involved with a married man for 14 years. When she finally left him, he responded by creating a fake Facebook profile and profiles on Sextrader and other escort sites (local and international) with nude photos of her and promoting her as a prostitute who would do anything and everything. The site said that they did not need to even make an appointment and could just arrive. He also provided an address for her, which is her mom's home address. She had men calling her and knocking on her mom's front door looking all hours of the day since the various profiles were launched in February 2014.
The photos were of her face super-imposed onto sexually explicit photos of other women's bodies. (But the public did not know that). She was very careful during their relationship never to show her face and naked body in the same image.
As a result of these profiles she changed her surname back to her maiden surname, changed her look and her mom has had to sell her house. She was first made aware of the profiles when she received an email notification, which she thinks her ex deliberately sent to her. She has documented all of the content and has managed (after much effort and the escort agencies initially refusing to remove her) to have her name and photos removed from Facebook and the escort agencies. She reported him to the police who said that they can't prove that he is responsible.. She did however trace the IP address to Bedfordview, where he is based but could not prove it is him..

INTERNATIONAL CASE STUDY: ANNMARIE CHIARINI
Annmarie Chiarini is a professor of English at a Maryland community college and the Victim Services Director for the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative (CCRI) and Endrevenge porn. In 2009 she ended a relationship and things got very ugly.. He was not going to take this break up gently. He was, as he put it, going to destroy me.
He created an eBay auction. The item up for bids? My body. All 88 pictures I had let him take over a 6-month period. He posted the link to the auction on the 5 Facebook pages of the college where I teach. He used my email account to send links to the auction to my ex-husband, babysitters, family, and friends. He mailed a printout of the auction page and a CD of the images to my son’s kindergarten teacher at the Catholic school he attends. He mailed the same to the chair of the English department at my college.
I was panicked and embarrassed. Focused on damage control, I fought with eBay to have the auction removed. Once one auction was taken down, he would start a new one under a new user name. I reported email abuse to Yahoo!, and pleaded with Facebook to have the links taken down. I contacted the senior administrators who maintain my college’s Facebook pages and asked them to take the links down and block him. I reached out to law enforcement officials in my county, but was repeatedly told there was nothing they could do because he had not committed a crime.
Damage control took precedence over eating, sleeping, my work, and sometimes even my children. After three weeks the auctions had been taken down, the links had been removed and Yahoo! Had “taken action” against him.
I blocked his and all his friends’ email addresses and phone numbers.
I had not had any contact with him in over 14 months.
Then, on 19 September, 2011, I received an email at work that a profile was made of me by someone acting as me that featured naked pictures of me. It was him. It had to be.
The profile featured my full name and the details of my place of employment. It made me a target. The tagline on the profile read, “Hot for teacher? Come and get it!” A solicitation. I was so terrified, I couldn’t leave my home for months .
I reported the impersonation to the web-hosting site, and it came down three days later. It had been active for 15 days and had over 3,000 views.
She received rape threats from men she had never met..
Again, law enforcement officials couldn’t help me. So I decided to change the laws.
In February 2012, she testified before the Judiciary Committee of the Maryland General Assembly in support of Senate Bills (SB) 107 and 175. SB 175 was passed into law in April 2012; it amended the current online harassment legislation, providing victims with stronger prosecuting ability. In 2014 Annmarie testified before the house committee and fought for legislation to make non-consensual pornography a crime. The law went into effect in October 2014. Non-consensual pornography is now a crime in Maryland. Annmarie is waiting to hear whether her lobbying efforts and testimony will result in Washington DC criminalizing non-consensual pornography.
Since her work with CCRI and EndRevengePorn, she has dealt with 2500 cases of revenge porn in 2.5 years. According to her, it is a form of sexual abuse.

metadata.Summary: The internet defies the law that what goes up must come down.. And many women are learning (the very hard way) that once explicit media of your most private moments goes up, it may never come down. Revenge porn is the unauthorized sharing of sexualized images, this happens most commonly across digital platforms. It is also largely categorized as digital sexual assault. It has become one of the most popular ways that disgruntled exes are taking out their anger on their former partners - by leaking their most private photos or videos online - naming and shaming the victims and sometimes even tagging the name of the company they work for and to their profiles on Facebook and Linked In etc. 95% of the victims are women. As with offline violence against women, the bulk of the abuse is at the hands not of strangers, but of people known to the women targeted. In the case of both of our case studies, their offenders were their former partners. There are 2000 sites dedicated to revenge porn. From myex.com (where men can post pics of their exes) to shesahomewrecker.com (where women name and shame their partners mistresses and it's run by a woman). The online world is being used as a weapon and the victims incur huge social, financial, psychological, emotional and professional costs. There are incidents of victims losing their jobs, receiving rape threats, having to move and even having to change their name. Revenge porn cases happen all around the world, to people across all ages and the topic has started to make international mainstream news and every day conversations. Putting pressure on judiciaries and social network platforms to change laws and regulations.
